In 1494, Spain and Portugal drew one line down the Atlantic and split the entire world between them.

No one else was consulted. Most of the planet hadn't even been mapped.

The Treaty of Tordesillas — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Columbus returns in 1493, and Spain rushes to the Pope to lock in its claims.

Conveniently, Alexander VI is a Spaniard — a Borgia. His bulls draw a line 100 leagues west of the Azores: everything beyond belongs to Castile.

Portugal, the era's naval superpower, is furious.

2/ Portugal threatens war, and in June 1494 the two crowns cut a private deal at Tordesillas: move the line to 370 leagues west of Cape Verde.

East of it — Africa and Asia — Portugal's half. West — the new lands — Spain's.

The Pope's line is simply renegotiated between kings.

3/ The line hid a surprise no one had mapped yet: the eastern bulge of South America poked across it.

In 1500, Pedro Álvares Cabral landed there and claimed it for Portugal.

That accident is why 200+ million Brazilians speak Portuguese on a Spanish-speaking continent.

4/ The treaty never said where the line ran on the OTHER side of the planet.

When both empires reached the Spice Islands from opposite directions in the 1520s, they had to draw a second line: the Treaty of Zaragoza, 1529.

Spain sold its claim to the Moluccas for 350,000 ducats.

5/ Everyone else ignored it. Francis I of France reportedly demanded to see "the clause in Adam's will" that excluded him.

England and the Netherlands simply sailed wherever they pleased — and built empires in the "wrong" halves.

6/ But the line left real fingerprints: Brazil's language, the Philippines' Spanish centuries, Portugal's African and Asian outposts held into the 1970s.

Two kingdoms, one meridian, half a millennium of consequences.
